formulas.name: Speed, distance and time
formulas.explanation: Speed is distance covered per unit of time. The same relation, rearranged, gives the distance (speed times time) or the journey time (distance divided by speed). Keep the units consistent: metres with seconds, or kilometres with hours.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for journey planning, running pace, and any motion at a steady or average speed.
assumptions: average speed over the whole journey

example.story: A car covers 150 km (150 000 m) in 2 hours (7200 s). What is its average speed?

formulas.name: Average speed over two stages
formulas.explanation: Average speed is always total distance divided by total time. It is generally not the average of the two speeds, because you spend longer at the slower speed. Driving there at 40 km/h and back at 60 km/h averages 48 km/h, not 50.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for journeys with several stages at different speeds.

example.story: A cyclist rides 60 km in 1 hour, then 40 km in half an hour. What is her average speed?

formulas.name: Kilometres per hour to metres per second
formulas.explanation: One kilometre per hour is 1000 m in 3600 s, which is 1/3.6 m/s. So divide km/h by 3.6 to get m/s, and multiply by 3.6 to go back. For miles per hour, 1 mph is about 0.447 m/s.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it before putting road speeds into physics formulas, which need m/s.

example.story: A car drives at 90 km/h. What is that in m/s?

formulas.name: Stopping distance of a vehicle

variables.name: reaction time
variables.description: Time before the brakes are applied (about 0.7 s, longer when tired or distracted).

variables.name: braking deceleration
variables.description: Size of the deceleration (about 6.7 m/s² on a dry road).

formulas.explanation: The car first travels at full speed during the driver's reaction time (thinking distance), then slows to a stop (braking distance, from v² = 2as). Braking distance grows with the square of the speed, so doubling the speed roughly quadruples it.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for road safety, safe following distances and speed limit discussions.

example.story: A car travels at 13.4 m/s (30 mph). The driver reacts in 0.67 s and brakes at 6.67 m/s². What is the stopping distance?

formulas.name: Fuel consumption (litres per 100 km)
formulas.explanation: Fuel consumption in Europe is quoted as litres per 100 km: lower is better. Divide the fuel used by the distance and scale to 100 km. In the US, miles per gallon is used instead, where higher is better.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to compare cars, check your own driving efficiency or estimate fuel costs.

example.story: A car uses 42 litres of fuel to drive 600 km. What is its fuel consumption?

formulas.name: Fuel cost of a trip

variables.name: fuel cost
variables.description: Cost of the fuel, in currency units.

formulas.explanation: The fuel needed is the distance divided by 100 times the consumption per 100 km. Multiplying by the price per litre gives the cost. Splitting it between passengers is then a simple division.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to budget for road trips or compare driving with other transport.

example.story: A 350 km trip in a car using 6.5 L/100 km, with fuel at 1.85 per litre. What does the fuel cost?

formulas.name: Cost of running an appliance

variables.name: power
variables.description: Power of the appliance in kilowatts.

formulas.explanation: Energy companies charge per kilowatt-hour, the energy used by a 1 kW appliance in one hour. Multiply the power in kW by the hours of use to get kWh, then by the price.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to compare appliances, estimate bills or see what standby power costs over a year.
assumptions: everyday units: kW, hours, price per kWh

example.story: A 2 kW heater runs for 3 hours with electricity at 0.30 per kWh. What does it cost?

formulas.name: Body mass index (BMI)
formulas.explanation: BMI compares body mass with height. Dividing by height squared makes tall and short adults roughly comparable. For adults, 18.5 to 25 is the usual healthy range, but BMI does not distinguish muscle from fat and does not apply directly to children.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it as a rough screening number for adults, not as a diagnosis.
assumptions: a population-level indicator; it ignores body composition

example.story: A person has a mass of 70 kg and a height of 1.75 m. What is their BMI?

formulas.name: Celsius to Fahrenheit
formulas.explanation: Water freezes at 0 °C = 32 °F and boils at 100 °C = 212 °F, so 100 Celsius degrees span 180 Fahrenheit degrees: each °C is 1.8 °F. Multiply by 9/5 and add 32; to go back, subtract 32 and multiply by 5/9. The scales agree at -40.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for weather forecasts, recipes and thermometers in different countries.

example.story: Normal body temperature is about 37 °C. What is that in °F?

formulas.name: Celsius to kelvin
formulas.explanation: The kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature, -273.15 °C. A step of one kelvin is the same size as one degree Celsius, so converting only means adding 273.15. Physics and chemistry formulas need kelvin.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it before every gas law, radiation or thermodynamics formula.

formulas.name: Unit price

variables.name: unit price
variables.description: Price per kilogram, litre or item.

variables.name: quantity
variables.description: Amount in the pack (kg, litres or items).

formulas.explanation: To compare packs of different sizes, divide each price by the amount it contains. The lowest unit price is the best value, although a bigger pack is only a bargain if you use it all.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to compare prices in the shop or online.
assumptions: quantities in the same unit for both packs

example.story: A 750 g box of cereal costs 2.49. What is the price per kilogram?

formulas.name: Sale price after a discount
formulas.explanation: A discount of d % means you pay (100 - d) % of the original price. Two discounts in a row multiply: 20 % off and then another 10 % off is 28 % off in total, not 30 %.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it in sales, coupons and price comparisons.

example.story: A jacket costing 80 is reduced by 25 %. What is the sale price?

formulas.name: Splitting a bill with a tip

variables.name: tip
variables.description: Tip as a percentage of the bill.

formulas.explanation: Add the tip by multiplying the bill by 1 + t/100, then divide equally among the people. Working out the total first and dividing once avoids rounding differences.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it at restaurants and for sharing group costs.

example.story: Four friends share a bill of 84 and add a 15 % tip. How much does each pay?

formulas.name: Map scale

variables.name: scale factor
variables.description: The k in a scale of 1 : k.

formulas.explanation: A map scale of 1 : k means one unit on the map is k of the same units in reality. Multiply map distances by k to get real distances and divide to go the other way. Areas scale by k², not k.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for maps, plans, architectural drawings and models.
assumptions: map and real distance in the same unit

example.story: On a 1 : 25 000 walking map, two villages are 4 cm (0.04 m) apart. How far apart are they really?

formulas.name: Scaling a recipe

variables.name: new amount
variables.description: Amount of the ingredient for the new number of servings.

variables.name: original servings
variables.description: Number of servings the recipe makes.

formulas.explanation: Ingredients are directly proportional to the number of servings. Multiply every amount by the same ratio of new to old servings. Baking times and pan sizes do not always scale the same way, so take care with large changes.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to cook for more or fewer people, or to mix any recipe-like proportions such as paint or concrete.

example.story: A recipe for 4 people uses 300 g of flour. How much flour is needed for 6 people?
